title: Self-collaboration Code Generation via ChatGPT
venue: ACM Transactions on Software Engineering and Methodology
extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of improving large language model performance on complex code-generation tasks. The authors argue that single LLM agents, even strong ones such as ChatGPT, struggle with complex software requirements, and they draw inspiration from human software-development teamwork to propose a self-collaboration approach in which multiple role-specialized LLM agents work together. The paper is not about education, literacy, K-12 learners, or reading outcomes, and therefore does not provide direct evidence relevant to generative AI effects on foundational reading in school settings.

The intervention studied is a multi-agent framework for code generation using role instructions. In the proposed setup, three ChatGPT-based agents play analyst, coder, and tester roles and collaborate sequentially using a software-development methodology inspired by the waterfall model. The analyst decomposes requirements and creates a high-level plan, the coder writes or revises code, and the tester reviews the code and produces test reports. The framework is evaluated on multiple code-generation benchmarks such as HumanEval, MBPP, APPS, and CoderEval, with comparisons against single-agent ChatGPT, GPT-4, code-specialized LLMs, and prompting baselines.

The population and context are benchmark tasks and software-development scenarios rather than human participants. Experiments are conducted using publicly available programming benchmarks and case studies involving repository-level or project-level code-generation tasks. No students, teachers, schools, or educational institutions are involved, and no classroom or school-supported intervention is implemented.

The main conclusion is that self-collaboration substantially improves code-generation performance relative to a single base LLM, including gains in Pass@1 across several benchmarks. The authors conclude that role-based multi-agent collaboration can help LLMs handle more complex software-development tasks. However, because this is a software-engineering paper with no educational sample or reading measures, it should be treated as out of scope for the target verification question on K-12 causal evidence for generative AI and foundational reading outcomes; at most, it is a non-educational adjacent technical paper rather than a near-miss education study.
quality_tier_rationale: This is an experimental benchmark paper in software engineering, not a K-12 causal study. It reports comparative performance on coding benchmarks with clear methods, but no educational population, no randomized classroom design, and limited relevance to the requested K-12 foundational reading evidence question.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper shows sizable positive effects on code-generation benchmark performance, but impact is outside education and not on K-12 reading or school-supported literacy outcomes. Thus impact for the target evidence framework is unclear/indirect rather than directly meaningful.

interventions.use_case: Multi-agent self-collaboration with ChatGPT/GPT-4 for software code generation, using analyst/coder/tester roles to improve code-writing performance on programming benchmarks.

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that a self-collaboration framework for LLM-based code generation improved benchmark code-generation performance relative to a single ChatGPT agent. Reported gains include Pass@1 improvements from 57.3 to 74.4 on HumanEval, 42.7 to 56.1 on HumanEval-ET, 52.2 to 68.2 on MBPP, and 36.8 to 49.5 on MBPP-ET, described as relative improvements of 29.9%-34.6%; on CoderEval average Pass@1 increased from 19.82 to 29.14 (relative +47.1%). These are software productivity/task-performance outcomes, not educational learning outcomes.
finding.measure: Code-generation task performance/productivity measured by Pass@1 on software engineering benchmarks (HumanEval, HumanEval-ET, MBPP, MBPP-ET, APPS, CoderEval)
finding.study_size: n=427 tasks (MBPP), n=164 tasks (HumanEval), n=1000 tasks subset (APPS interview/competition), CoderEval task count not_reported in excerpt
finding.effect_size: relative improvement 29.9%-47.1% Pass@1 vs base LLM agent; absolute examples: HumanEval +17.1 points, HumanEval-ET +13.4 points, MBPP +16.0 points, MBPP-ET +12.7 points, CoderEval average +9.32 points
